maya.text:
Every generation of students has been told that the schoolhouse gate is where their rights stop being their own. The First Amendment limits what government may do, and a public school is government. The Supreme Court said as much in 1969, and then spent fifty years narrowing what it had said. The Court has not struck the right balance. It has drifted toward school authority, and it has done so by carving exceptions rather than by revisiting the rule.

Tinker v. Des Moines is still the standard, and it is a demanding one. Justice Fortas wrote that students do not "shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate," and the Court refused to accept the district's guesses about disruption. School officials had to show something.

Bethel v. Fraser is where the drift starts. Chief Justice Burger drew a "marked distinction" between Fraser's speech and the political speech in Tinker, and out of that distinction the Court built a category of speech schools may punish without showing any disruption at all. The reasoning is about vulgarity, but the effect is about power.

Someone will say schools cannot function if every rule becomes a constitutional case, and that is fair. Hazelwood is the strongest version of that argument: a school-sponsored newspaper is the school speaking, and the school may edit it. Justice Brennan answered it in dissent, writing that educators "must accommodate some student expression, even if it offends them." He was writing in dissent, which is why he could name the thing the majority needed to leave vague.

Mahanoy is the case that shows the Court knows it went too far. Eight justices held that a school could not punish a student for a Saturday Snapchat. The opinion is narrow, but it is the first time in decades the Court moved back toward the student, and it did so by returning to Tinker's question.

Tinker asked schools to prove something. The exceptions ask students to prove something instead.

devon.text:
Free speech in schools is a very important issue that many people have argued about over the years. The Supreme Court has made several decisions about it and they are all different.

In Tinker v. Des Moines the Court said students do not "shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate." This was about armbands and the Vietnam War. Later cases like Bethel and Hazelwood went the other way.

Overall the Supreme Court has tried to balance both sides. Both students and schools have a point. That is why this issue is still being discussed today.
